question: A pedestrian struck by a car at moderate speed shows a bumper fracture of the tibiae bilaterally at 45 cm above heel level, diffuse scalp contusions on the opposite side of the head, and road abrasions on the hands and knees. Which sequence of impact events best explains these findings?

answers.text: The victim was thrown under the car and run over, then dragged.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Run-over would produce tyre tread abrasions and crush injuries to larger body segments, not a classic bumper-level tibial fracture followed by contrecoup-pattern scalp injury. The bilateral tibial fracture at a defined height is characteristic of primary bumper contact, not run-over.

answers.text: Primary impact by the bumper fractured the tibiae; secondary impact against the bonnet/windscreen caused the contralateral scalp contusion; tertiary impact on the road caused the abrasions.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Waddell's triad in pedestrians: (1) Primary bumper impact fractures the long bones (tibiae) at bumper height; (2) The body vaults forward, and the head/trunk strikes the bonnet or windscreen — contralateral scalp contusion is the contre-coup secondary impact; (3) The victim falls to the road, producing palm and knee abrasions from the tertiary impact.

answers.text: All injuries were sustained simultaneously from a single high-speed impact.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Vehicular pedestrian injuries follow a predictable sequential pattern — not simultaneous. Recognising the sequence is critical to reconstructing speed, direction of vehicle travel, and whether the victim was struck from front or rear.

answers.text: The abrasions indicate the victim was dragged; the tibial fractures resulted from kicking during a struggle.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dragging injuries produce long linear patterned abrasions with tissue loss in the direction of dragging — not palm and knee abrasions consistent with a fall to the road surface. The bilateral tibial fractures at bumper height are not consistent with a kick mechanism.

overallFeedback.feedback: Pedestrian-vehicle injuries follow a three-step sequence: primary (bumper — long bone fractures at bumper height), secondary (bonnet/windscreen — upper body and head injury), tertiary (road surface — abrasions from the fall). Reconstruct each step separately in your report.

Accurate reconstruction. Waddell's triad (bumper fracture → bonnet/windscreen contact → road fall) is the classic pedestrian injury sequence. Document bumper height meticulously — it can identify the class of vehicle involved.
